claims.text: Heating sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles to 1000 K in vacuum causes structural evolution dominated by surface-energy minimization and rapid surface diffusion.
The particles undergo kinetic phase separation and Ostwald ripening rather than bulk-HEA sluggish diffusion.
Below 10 nm, surface diffusion coefficients exceed bulk diffusion coefficients by orders of magnitude.
The configurational entropy of the five-component alloy is insufficient to overcome mixing-enthalpy and surface-energy contributions.
Au-Pt and Cu-Ni are specific negative-mixing-enthalpy binary pairs relevant to phase separation in this alloy.
The as-synthesized particles are likely metastable solid solutions or partially segregated.
A minutes-to-hours heating interval is sufficient for diffusion during the ramp to 1000 K.
The high surface-to-volume ratio creates a dominant mass-transport driving force that bypasses bulk lattice-diffusion barriers.
Surface-diffusion activation energies in sub-10 nm particles are significantly lower than bulk-diffusion activation energies.
Higher curvature raises the chemical potential of smaller particles, causing them to dissolve and redeposit onto larger particles by Ostwald ripening.
Sufficiently strong enthalpic interactions can overcome configurational entropy and produce non-random phases.
Strong negative mixing enthalpy and high surface mobility cause surface segregation or core-shell formation.
The sluggish-diffusion effect relies on lattice distortion and high activation barriers for bulk diffusion.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will disappear within the first 10–30 minutes of heating.
Heating will produce Au-Pt-rich and Cu-Ni-rich core-shell or otherwise segregated regions rather than a uniform solid solution.
Heating will reduce particle number and increase average particle size, potentially leaving one large particle per original cluster.
Under a sluggish-diffusion baseline, the equiatomic solid solution and particle-size distribution would remain substantially unchanged up to 1000 K.
The surface-diffusion regime applies below 10 nm, whereas bulk diffusion may dominate above 50 nm.
Vacuum prevents oxidation and thereby isolates surface-energy effects.
Bulk-diffusion-controlled growth follows a t^(1/3) law, whereas surface-diffusion-controlled growth follows t^(1/2) or faster kinetics.
